q: What collective nickname have Ike, Yamauchi, and Sudou earned after three weeks of school?
a: They are collectively known as the 'Idiot Trio.'

q: How do the teachers respond to students chatting, arriving late, or sleeping in class?
a: Out of some laissez-faire feeling they tolerate everything - no one cares about poor language, lateness, or dozing, though a few students like Horikita study diligently.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: What rumor about Hirata is circulating in the class?
a: That he is dating Karuizawa; Hondou saw them holding hands and walking together shoulder to shoulder, and Hirata confirms they are dating.

q: What is unusual about the short test Chiyabashira gives at the end of the month?
a: It covers five subjects with four questions each worth five points, is explicitly not reflected in report cards, and its final three questions are an order of magnitude harder than the rest.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: Why does Ayanokouji find the pop quiz's phrasing suspicious?
a: Chiyabashira emphasizes it will not affect report cards, which makes him think the grade could be reflected in some other way instead.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: How does Ayanokouji handle the difficult final questions on the surprise test?
a: He quietly solves them the same way he did on the entrance exam while Horikita's pen dances across her paper toward a perfect score.

q: How badly has Yamauchi managed his points within three weeks?
a: He has almost nothing left - about 2,000 points - after blowing over 90,000, including roughly 20,000 (25,000 with extras) on a PS Viva handheld bought jointly with Ike.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: What free options exist for students who run out of points?
a: The vending machine has a free mineral water button, and the cafeteria offers a free vegetable meal set that Yamauchi scoffs at.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: Who joins the after-class outing that Kushida assembles?
a: Besides Ike, Yamauchi and Ayanokouji, Kushida brings Hirata and Karuizawa along with Karuizawa's friends Matsushita and Mori.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: Why do Ike and Yamauchi resent Hirata joining the hangout?
a: They fear the popular pretty boy will overshadow them and might steal Kushida's attention, despite him already dating Karuizawa.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: What did Karuizawa purchase during the campus trip and how much did it cost?
a: She bought clothes costing about 30,000 points, which Hirata carried for her.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: How do the classmates differ in their feelings about the monthly allowance?
a: Karuizawa and Ike wish they had more points, even 200,000 or 300,000 a month, while Hirata and Kushida are terrified about what will happen when the luxurious life ends.

q: What embarrassing mistake does Yamauchi make about a standardized test?
a: He boasts of scoring 900 on 'the APEC'; Kushida corrects him that he means the TOEIC, since APEC actually stands for Asia-Pacific Economic Partnership.

source: Chapter 6: The End of Everyday Life
q: What question lingers with Ayanokouji after the group outing?
a: If the school does not choose students solely on test scores, how does it select them? He finds himself suddenly curious.

q: What shocking discovery do Hondou and others make on May 1?
a: No points were deposited into their accounts despite it being the first of the month, though Chiyabashira insists the transfer went through without issues.

q: How does Kouenji explain the missing point deposits?
a: He smugly concludes that because they are Class D, they received not a single point this month.

q: What infractions caused Class D to forfeit its entire monthly allowance?
a: A total of ninety-eight absences and late arrivals plus three hundred ninety-one incidences of talking or using cell phones in class over one month.

q: How does Chiyabashira justify giving zero points without prior explanation?
a: She says students learned in elementary school that being late and talking in class are bad, so claiming ignorance is flimsy reasoning - it comes down to personal responsibility.

q: What cruel detail does Chiyabashira reveal about next month's points?
a: Even if no one is ever late again, zero points will still be deposited next month - fixing behavior stops deductions but produces no increases.

q: What are the class point totals posted after the first month?
a: Class A has 940, Class B 650, Class C 490, and Class D 0, where 1,000 points equals 100,000 yen; Horikita and Ayanokouji both notice the numbers look suspiciously even.

q: How are students actually sorted into classes at this school?
a: Students are sorted by level of excellence like at major cram schools - the superior go to Class A and the least capable to Class D, making D the last bastion for failures.

q: What dubious distinction does this year's Class D hold?
a: It is the first class in school history to spend all of its points within a single month.

q: Can Class D recover from zero points?
a: The balance remains at zero until graduation, but students are assured they will not die - dorms and free meals remain available.

q: What do class points signify besides money?
a: They indicate class rank; reaching 500 points would promote Class D to Class C, working like a company performance review.

q: What were the results of the earlier short test?
a: The average was sixty-five; Sudou scored fourteen and Ike twenty-four; seven students fell below the red line, with Kikuchi highest among failures at thirty-one points.

q: Which two students tied for the top score on the short test?
a: Kouenji and Yukimura, both scoring ninety - meaning Kouenji solved one of the super difficult problems.

q: What rule about failing exams does Chiyabashira reveal?
a: Anyone who fails a midterm or final exam must drop out of school; applied to the practice test, everyone below thirty-two points would have been expelled.

q: According to Chiyabashira, what must Class D do to secure its desired future?
a: Only by overtaking Class A can students guarantee advancement into their college or workplace of choice; the school guarantees nothing for any other class.

q: Why is Kouenji unbothered by being placed in Class D?
a: He believes the school simply has not seen his potential yet, his future leading the Kouenji conglomerate is already decided, and he is certain the school would come begging if he dropped out.

q: How does Kushida defuse the confrontation between Yukimura and Hirata?
a: She slips between them, gently takes Yukimura's balled fist, and reasons that banding together is better than fighting, calming him almost completely.

q: What evidence-gathering do Ayanokouji and Horikita do after learning about the point system?
a: Ayanokouji photographs the class point totals poster while Horikita tallies the class's absences, tardiness, and talking incidents in her notebook, both trying to reverse-engineer the formula.

q: What plan does Hirata propose to the class, and who refuses to join?
a: He urges everyone to stop arriving late, talking, and using phones to earn points back; Sudou sneers and storms out, Horikita refuses as meaningless, and Ayanokouji also declines.

q: What hint does Horikita drop about her attitude toward the class system?
a: She says she cannot meekly accept her current situation, then falls completely silent when asked what she means.

q: Who is Hoshinomiya Chie?
a: The Class B homeroom teacher, best friends with Chiyabashira since high school, flirtatious toward Ayanokouji until Chiyabashira smacks her with a clipboard.

q: Which beautiful student comes to fetch Hoshinomiya during the faculty office scene?
a: Ichinose, a girl with light-pink hair, arrives saying the student council wishes to discuss something with her teacher.

q: Why does Chiyabashira hide Ayanokouji in the guidance room kitchenette?
a: She engineers him overhearing Horikita's protest about her Class D placement, deeming it necessary for both students to hear what follows.

q: What is Horikita's academic record from the entrance examination?
a: She solved nearly every problem, had the third-highest score among first-year students, and made no substantial mistakes in her interview, yet was still sorted into Class D.

q: What critique of Japanese society does Chiyabashira offer regarding merit-based ranking?
a: Relying solely on test scores let incompetents at the top kick down truly superior students, so society settled on a system of hereditary succession instead.

q: Why might some students prefer being evaluated low, according to Chiyabashira?
a: Class A lives under incredible pressure from the school and extreme envy from lower classes, so some strange students happily accept a low evaluation.

q: What pattern in Ayanokouji's test scores exposes him?
a: He scored exactly fifty in every subject and on the short quiz, perfectly solved the fifth math problem that only 3 percent solve using complex formulae, yet botched the tenth problem that 76 percent complete - evidence of deliberate calibration.

q: How does Chiyabashira compare Ayanokouji to Horikita?
a: She suggests he may be even more intelligent than Horikita, causing Horikita to flinch.

q: What joke does Chiyabashira make about E Class?
a: When Ayanokouji threatens to go mad and destroy the furniture, she says she would demote him to E Class - where E stands for expelled.

q: What three immediate problems does Horikita identify facing Class D?
a: Tardiness, talking during class, and ensuring no one fails the upcoming midterm exam.

q: What shogi analogy does Horikita use to explain why she wants Ayanokouji specifically?
a: She does not need a gold or silver general right now - she wants a pawn - and calls him the only person in Class D easy enough to manipulate.

q: How does Horikita react when Ayanokouji refuses to help her?
a: She ignores the refusal entirely, saying she always knew he would help and claiming to hear the voice inside his head.
